title: A working hypothesis visualization method for fNIRS measurements using Monte Carlo simulation
author: Kikuchi, Nomura
materials: Finger tapping, which is a basic task in many papers, was adopted as the measurement task in this study [2], [3], [4]. Finger tapping has the advantage of eliminating movements other than fingertips. Furthermore, it is thought that the activation area tends to appear remarkably and stably because the measurement can be performed in a relaxed state with little emotional fluctuation. In this study, finger tapping was performed by tapping the thumb and index finger. Tapping task was performed with the left and right hands in sequence. Fig. 1(A) shows the paradigm design. Protocol began with 20 s rest period as a baseline. Afterwards, finger tapping was performed for 20 s. After each tapping segment, rest period was provided for 20 s, and this cycle was repeated 5 times. Two sets of experiments were performed with the right and left hands, respectively. Also, tapping movement was performed at a pace of approximately 1 Hz during the task period. At this time, the computer monitor displayed a signal to start and finish the task, and the subject changed their behavior according to the signal.Fig. 1Study design. (A) Experimental paradigm. (B) fNIRS optode layout design. (C) Lateral view of the corresponding anatomical regions of channel configuration.Fig 1

steps.title: Obtain ethics approval and consent
steps.instruction: Confirm that the study has ethics committee approval (protocol 23‑006) and obtain written informed consent from the participant (male, 60 years old, right‑handed, no neurological history).

steps.title: Seat participant and prepare
steps.instruction: Seat the subject on a chair, ask them to remain as still as possible, and focus on the computer monitor during data collection.

steps.title: Place fNIRS optodes
steps.instruction: Arrange the fNIRS probe on the right and left head surfaces according to the 7 × 3 optode layout (Fig. 1B) and secure it for the upcoming measurement.

steps.title: Run finger‑tapping paradigm
steps.instruction: Execute the following sequence for each hand (right hand first, then left hand): start with a 20 s rest baseline, then a 20 s tapping block at ~1 Hz (thumb‑index tapping), followed by a 20 s rest; repeat this tap‑rest cycle 5 times. The computer monitor displays start/stop cues that the subject follows.

steps.title: Collect fNIRS data
steps.instruction: Record continuous fNIRS signals (HbO) from all channels during the entire paradigm, ensuring data are saved for later analysis.

steps.title: Preprocess data with NIRS‑SPM
steps.instruction: Load the raw data into NIRS‑SPM and apply the internal preprocessing pipeline:

substeps.instruction: Wavelet‑MDL detrending (high‑pass filter) to remove respiration, heart‑rate, vasomotion, and other global trends.
Hemodynamic response function (HRF) pre‑coloring to correct the HbO time‑courses.

steps.title: Perform GLM analysis
steps.instruction: Using NIRS‑SPM, run a general linear model on the preprocessed HbO signals with the canonical HRF, modeling the task condition versus baseline (default settings).

substeps.instruction: Use a significance threshold of p < 0.05.
Generate t‑statistic maps and overlay them on the MNI152 standard brain.

steps.title: Create simulation activation colormaps
steps.instruction: From the Monte‑Carlo simulation, obtain ΔHbO values for each channel and produce 2‑D activation maps:

substeps.instruction: Map ΔHbO values onto the 7 × 3 channel grid (Fig. 2A/D).
Linearly interpolate values for grid positions without data (Fig. 2B/E).
Apply a second linear interpolation over the entire grid to generate a high‑resolution 2‑D activation colormap (Fig. 2C/F) using the provided MATLAB script activationmap.m.

steps.title: Reconstruct measured t‑value maps in 2‑D
steps.instruction: Take the channel‑wise t‑values from NIRS‑SPM (Fig. S3) and reconstruct them into 2‑D maps using the same interpolation method as for the simulation (Fig. 2).

steps.title: Compute centroids of activation maps
steps.instruction: Run the MATLAB program activationmap.m to calculate the centroid of each 2‑D activation map (both simulation ΔHbO and measured t‑value maps).

substeps.instruction: Overlay the 2‑D channel coordinates (x, y) with their corresponding MNI coordinates (x, y, z) obtained via NIRS‑SPM probabilistic registration.
Use MATLAB’s scatteredInterpolant to interpolate the MNI coordinates across the 2‑D map and locate the centroid in 3‑D space.
Identify the anatomical region of each centroid with the AAL atlas via NIRS‑SPM’s probabilistic registration function.

steps.title: Compare simulation and measurement centroids
steps.instruction: Report the Euclidean distance between the simulation centroid and the measured centroid for each hand (e.g., 8.7 mm for right‑hand tapping, 7.7 mm for left‑hand tapping) and note that both lie in the precentral gyrus.
